newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: REITH APPEALS FOR IR UNIFORMITY
The Commonwealth's attempts to establish an integrated industrial relations system across Australia will continue today at a meeting of the nation's industrial relations ministers.
Federal Minister, Peter Reith, wants the states to pass complementary laws to support his Workplace Relations Act.
Mr Reith wants the states to pass uniform laws on unfair dismissals and certified agreements, and wants the employment advocate to have responsibility for workers' complaints raised under state laws.
He'll also be asking the states and territories to reduce to 20 the number of items included in industrial awards.
Six months ago, state ministers agreed to work to ensure greater consistency between their own systems, and federal law.
But while the conservative states are expected to embrace Mr Reith's plan today, a cool reception is expected from the Labor Government in New South Wales.
MINING IN FORESTS TO BE GIVEN GO-AHEAD
The Federal Government's shed some light on its plans to move to what it's called multiple land use for forest reserves.
Under the plan, forest reserves will be classified as dedicated or informal.
Mining will be allowed in informal reserves, which will be less environmentally significant than dedicated reserves.
But states will still be allowed to permit mining in dedicated reserves if the Commonwealth agrees.
The plan has come in for criticism.
Shadow Environment Minister, Carmen Lawrence, says mining interest are being put ahead of the protection of forests.
The Australian Conservation Foundation says environment policy is being run by resources ministers.
And the Minerals Council says it's disappointed that mineral exploration will be virtually banned in some forests.
NO FEES ON SOME ANZ TRANSACTIONS TOMORROW
Some across-the-counter ANZ Bank fees such as those on cheques, bank drafts, and international transfers won't be charged tomorrow because of industrial action.
It's part of a continuing dispute by members of the Finance Sector Union over job security and redundancy packages.
The Union's Tony Beck says the bank's recorded its second successive billion dollar profit, and can afford a 25 per cent pay rise for it's top executive.
But he says it can't assure workers about their jobs.
He says the union wants to reach an agreement about a fair and equitable way in which jobs will be terminated.
STATUS OF WOMEN BOSS RESIGNS
The head of the Federal Office of the Status of Women Kathy Townsend has resigned after two and half years in the job.
Ms Townsend has accepted a position in the private sector in Melbourne.
She says she's confident of the Coalition government's commitment to the Office.
Ms Townshend says she's had every assurance the office will continue and the government will be looking for her replacement as soon as possible.
APPEAL DISMISSED OVER SUITCASE MURDERS
The Court of Criminal Appeal has dismissed an appeal by a man who was convicted of murdering two women, and putting their bodies in suitcases.

Edwin Thomas Street of Sydney, was convicted of killing his wife Dawn by suffocating her after an argument in November 1993. The next morning her body was put in a suitcase and she was buried in a reserve at Wollstonecraft.
Three months later police found the body of a woman Street had been living with since his wife's death, in a suitcase.
Street appealed on the basis the trial judge erred in allowing a joint trial for the murders, but the court found the trial judge was not in error.
Street's appeal against his life sentence, was also dismissed.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
